brief: A portable electronics organizer: a base with removable bins for small parts, at least one drawer, and a carry handle.

requirements.evidence: piece:0,0,0;full and piece:0,1,0;half-n, locked together with jointBolt:0#0,0#5 and capped on every open face

bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-half-div2 (2 compartments) and bin:0,1,0~hex-bin-half-n-third-div3 (3 compartments) are separate bin parts that lift out of the bases. Each sits under a lid (cover:0,0,0;full;top and cover:0,1,0;half-n;top), so you take the lid off to reach them.
drawer:0#0,1#cut on the cut face of the half base, shown open with a heap of nuts inside
handle:0,0,0;top on the top cover of the full base, held by 3 inserts

It is small (two cells) and has a top handle with the joints bolted. The configurator checks fit only, not strength, so it can't confirm the handle and joints will hold the loaded organizer when it is carried.

finish.summary: I built a compact two-cell electronics organizer with 29 parts, about 1276 g of filament and about 1839 minutes of printing. It has a full hex base and a north half base, with lift-out bins under lids, a drawer, a carry handle on top, caps on the open faces and a joint bolt locking the two bases together. The configurator checks passed with no rule errors and no mesh collisions. For staging, I put a heap of M3 screws in one bin compartment and a heap of M3 nuts in the open drawer. The screws are hidden under the lid in the normal view.

M3 x 10 socket head screw, ISO 4762
M6 x 20 socket head screw, ISO 4762
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
